ai.title: Maxilla Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The maxilla forms the upper jaw and palate, supporting teeth and facial structures. Understanding its relationships, blood and nerve supply, and common pathologies is essential for diagnosis and surgical planning in low‑resource settings.

b: Supports 12 upper teeth per side
Forms floor of the nasal cavity and part of the orbital floor
Key landmark for dental, ENT and maxillofacial surgery
sections.p: The maxilla is a paired, irregular bone that makes up the central portion of the facial skeleton, forming the upper dental arch, hard palate, and part of the orbit.

b: Body: central bulk containing the sinus
Alveolar process: tooth sockets
Palatine process: posterior hard palate
Frontal process: contributes to the nasal bridge
sections.p: Each maxilla has a body, four processes (frontal, zygomatic, alveolar, and palatine), and a sinus cavity (maxillary sinus). The alveolar process holds the teeth; the palatine process forms the hard palate.

b: Posteriorly: maxillary tuberosity contacts the pterygoid process of the sphenoid
Laterally: zygomatic process contacts the zygomatic bone
Medially: forms part of the nasal cavity floor
sections.p: The maxilla articulates with nine bones: frontal, nasal, zygomatic, lacrimal, ethmoid, sphenoid, palatine, vomer, and the opposite maxilla via the intermaxillary suture.

b: Infraorbital artery (branch of maxillary artery) supplies the anterior wall and palate
Posterior superior alveolar artery supplies the posterior alveolar bone and sinus
sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the maxilla primarily through branches of the external carotid system.

b: Infraorbital nerve supplies the skin over the cheek and the mucosa of the upper lip
Posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies posterior teeth and sinus mucosa
sections.p: Sensory innervation is via branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2).

b: Anchors muscles of mastication (e.g., masseter via the zygomatic process)
Forms part of the airway and contributes to resonance
sections.p: The maxilla provides structural support for the upper dentition, contributes to speech articulation, mastication, and protects the nasal cavity and orbital floor.

b: Le Fort fractures: classification based on level of maxillary separation
Maxillary sinusitis: may follow upper respiratory infection or dental infection
Erythroid hyperplasia (e.g., in sickle cell disease) can cause bone expansion and facial deformity
Osteomyelitis of the maxilla: higher risk with HIV, diabetes, or malnutrition
sections.p: Maxillary fractures, infections, and developmental anomalies are common in low‑resource settings, often linked to trauma, poor dental hygiene, or systemic disease.

t.b: Detects sinus opacification or displaced fracture fragments; if unavailable, use clinical signs of facial swelling and crepitus
Provides detailed fracture mapping; when absent, rely on physical exam and plain films
Identifies bacterial cause of sinusitis; if lab unavailable, treat empirically for common organisms (Streptococcus, anaerobes) and consider TB in endemic areas

b: Palpable step-off or mobility of the midface suggests Le Fort fracture
Periorbital ecchymosis (Raccoon eyes) indicates possible basal skull fracture involving the maxilla
Tenderness over the maxillary sinus with purulent nasal discharge points to sinusitis
sections.p: Key bedside findings guide diagnosis when imaging is limited.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe facial swelling with airway compromise
Uncontrolled epistaxis from a maxillary fracture
Rapidly spreading facial cellulitis or necrotizing infection
